title: Injective, surjective, or clean?
intro: Every system below maps inputs to outputs. Diagnose which algebraic property it loses — and note that the two failures cost you different things.

buckets.label: Surjectivity lost
buckets.hint: An output nothing reaches — capacity wasted

cards.text: A keypad encoder where Key_A and Key_B both drive register 0x01
A hydraulic ram clipping at ±10°: every stick angle past 5° gives the same deflection
A 12-bit quantiser fed a signal with 16 bits of real resolution
An API gateway routing /users, /orders and /cart to three distinct services — while PaymentSvc has no route at all
An enum with a case the parser can never emit
A fly-by-wire linkage: three column positions, three distinct actuator extensions, full range swept
Serialize then encrypt: each payload becomes its own packet, and the receiver recovers every one exactly
A lookup table pairing every scan code with exactly one command, and every command with exactly one code

debrief: The cost structures are genuinely different, which is why the two failures are worth telling apart. **Injectivity failure destroys information**: after two keys collide on 0x01, no downstream stage can tell which was pressed — the quantiser and the saturating ram are the same crime with better press. **Surjectivity failure wastes capacity**: PaymentSvc is deployed, running and billed, and unreachable. It costs money, not correctness, and it usually survives review because nothing fails. Note also what makes the bijective cases bijective: each pairs a domain and a codomain of the same size with nothing left over — which is exactly the condition for an inverse to exist, and the reason a serialize-then-encrypt chain round-trips while an anti-aliasing filter does not.
